query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticle stability at high temperatures is governed by kinetically driven surface segregation that results in the rapid formation of a protective oxide (or intermetallic) layer. This segregated layer acts as a diffusion barrier, preserving the nanoparticle’s internal solid-solution structure under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles produced via physical and chemical fabrication techniques, initially exhibiting a homogeneous alloy structure.
generation.intervention: Controlled annealing experiments on size-selected nanoparticles under variable atmospheres, with in situ environmental TEM and operando X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) used to monitor surface segregation, oxide or intermetallic layer formation, and phase evolution in real time.
generation.conditions: Annealing at high temperatures corresponding to catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) regimes, under controlled atmospheres such as oxidizing, inert, and reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The selectively segregated surface layer (oxide or intermetallic) that forms during controlled annealing, which limits further elemental diffusion and prevents deleterious core restructuring.
generation.mechanism: Selective elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surface, favored by specific annealing conditions, leads to the formation of a kinetically stabilized surface compound. This compound acts as a self-healing barrier against oxidation and phase transformation at high temperature, similar to protective layers observed in bulk alloys under analogous conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles subjected to controlled annealing will exhibit the rapid formation of a consistent, protective surface layer that correlates with improved structural and chemical stability during high-temperature exposure. In contrast, nanoparticles produced via conventional synthesis without this tailored annealing treatment will show uncontrolled phase evolution and faster degradation.
generation.baseline: Conventionally synthesized nanoparticles that have not undergone controlled annealing and (therefore) lack the purposefully formed protective surface layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in multi-element, near-equiatomic systems where there is sufficient difference in the oxidation or segregation tendencies among constituent elements. It may not apply if the elemental composition does not permit formation of an effective protective layer or if the nanoparticles are too small/large such that surface area effects dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal composition and thickness of the protective surface layer required for maximum stability are not yet fully determined. Additionally, the interplay between particle size, precise elemental diffusivities, and atmosphere composition introduces uncertainty in scaling the effect across different nanoparticle systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a set of annealing experiments on size-selected nanoparticles in both oxidizing and inert atmospheres at the target temperatures. Monitor the evolution of the surface layer in situ using TEM and operando XPS for nanoparticles processed under controlled conditions versus those processed via conventional methods.
measurements: Surface composition and thickness measured by operando XPS
Real-time imaging of layer formation and phase evolution via environmental TEM
Assessment of catalytic activity or thermoelectric performance to determine the correlation with structural stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the controlled annealing does not lead to a discernible, stable protective surface layer that correlates with enhanced nanoparticle stability (as measured by consistent catalytic/thermoelectric performance and structural integrity) relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that kinetically driven surface segregation governs stability is falsified.

First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].

Chen et al. [ [12] ] assessed the tensile performance of the equiatomic NbMoCrTiAl HEA at temperatures ranging from 800 °C to 1200 °

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . decision.trend: Early work on multi‐element, near‐equiatomic alloys largely focused on bulk and film systems produced by arc melting and powder metallurgy. These studies observed that slight variations in processing (e.g., melting temperature, annealing time, and cooling rate) significantly impacted phase formation, oxidation kinetics, and microstructural evolution under high‐temperature and reactive conditions. For example, research on oxidation (PMC6317005) demonstrated that oxidation behavior changes markedly with temperature due to scale formation and breakaway kinetics, while work on additive manufactured refractory alloys (PMC11077685) showed that controlled processing can yield dense, single-phase structures with improved oxidation resistance. However, the controlled selection of synthesis parameters for nanoparticles has not yet been linked mechanistically to preservation of structural and chemical stability in high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric applications.
decision.unsolved: What remains unsolved is the lack of a clear, mechanistic synthesis–structure–property relationship at the nanoparticle scale. In particular, it is unknown how synthesis conditions (e.g., energy input, annealing atmosphere, and particle size) govern surface segregation and the formation of protective oxide or intermetallic layers that can stabilize the nanoparticle core under service conditions.
decision.lever: Perform controlled annealing experiments on size-selected nanoparticles under variable atmospheres combined with in situ environmental TEM and operando X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to monitor surface segregation, oxide layer formation, and phase evolution in real time.
decision.why: This approach directly leverages the trend seen in bulk and film studies—where processing dramatically influences oxidation and phase stability—but applies it to the nanoparticle regime. In situ characterization will enable the mechanistic discrimination of whether kinetically stabilized surfaces (via selective segregation/oxide formation) are responsible for preserving structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions, providing a clear falsification test by comparing in situ evolution against a baseline of conventionally synthesized nanoparticles.
